entry.summary: This year’s holiday season is more special than usual. Olivia Rodrigo — who released her awesome third album you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love in June — is sharing her first-ever Christmas song. It’s here now, and it’s titled “take me home (4 christmas).” “take me home (4 christmas)” was produced…
entry.content:
This year's holiday season is more special than usual. Olivia Rodrigo — who released her awesome third album you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love in June — is sharing her first-ever Christmas song. It's here now, and it's titled "take me home (4 christmas)."

"take me home (4 christmas)" was produced by Dan Nigro, who wrote it with Rodrigo and Amy Allen. It follows last month's playful "expectations" remix with Chappell Roan, which came with a (not-AI-generated!) music video featuring David Byrne. "take me home (4 christmas)" also comes with a music video, and this one features Sex And The City's Cynthia Nixon and SNL's Ben Marshall.

Earlier this year, Rodrigo told Jimmy Fallon that Sex And The City is her favorite show and it even inspired the album: "Like, when Miranda and Steve are getting back together, she's crying. 'Steve, anytime something funny happens, I just want to tell you.' And I remember watching that and being like, 'Oh, my God, I have to write a song about this,'" she said, seemingly alluding to "maggots for brains," which has the line: "And everything that's funny, I wish I could tell to him."

Watch the "take me home (4 christmas)" video below.

entry.title: Vatican’s Culture Minister Details Bob Dylan’s Audience With Pope
entry.summary: Bob Dylan met the Pope on Wednesday. It wasn’t the first time. Back in 1997, Dylan performed “Knockin’ On Heaven’s Door” in front of Pope John Paul II and about 300,000 young folks at the Eucharistic Congress in Bologna. Twenty-nine years later, he had an audience at the Vatican with Pope Leo XIV, the Chicago…
entry.content:
Bob Dylan met the Pope on Wednesday. It wasn't the first time. Back in 1997, Dylan performed "Knockin' On Heaven's Door" in front of Pope John Paul II and about 300,000 young folks at the Eucharistic Congress in Bologna. Twenty-nine years later, he had an audience at the Vatican with Pope Leo XIV, the Chicago native who has emerged as a lover of the arts and a critic of AI while advocating for social justice at every turn.

The images have been all over my social media timelines: the Pope in his white robe and skullcap, Dylan in his black hoodie (with the hood up, like he's been wearing it onstage at his shows) over top of a white dress shirt and tie. As Jokermen cohost Ian Grant put it in GQ, "Bob Dylan Dressed Like Timothée Chalamet To Meet The Pope."

Today, Substack's foremost Dylanologist Ray Padgett has secured some inside information about the meetup as well as Dylan's fellow music icon Patti Smith's recent audience with Pope Leo. At his Dylan newsletter Flagging Down The Double E's, Padgett interviewed Antonio Spadaro, the man who arranged the meetings. Spadaro is a Jesuit priest who serves as undersecretary of the Dicastery for Culture and Education of the Holy See, and he wrote his own Substack post about the Dylan/Leo summit — in Italian, naturally.

Spadaro met Smith in Amsterdam a few years ago at an event by the Nexus Institute, and they stayed in touch. He said he's spoken with her extensively about Pope Leo and his predecessor, Pope Francis. "I could tell she would love to meet him, and the Pope was glad to meet her," Spadaro told Padgett. His summary of their meeting:

It was July 31. When she sat down across the desk from him, all she said was “Hi,” almost in a whisper, and he laughed and said “Hi” back. Anyone who knows “Wave,” the song in which Patti imagines talking with John Paul I, knows that’s exactly how it begins. From there came a conversation of about forty minutes. Two people born in Chicago discovering they were old friends, sharing words, music, dreams, and hopes.

Here's Smith, Spadaro, and Pope Leo together:

Spadaro wouldn't say whose idea it was for Dylan to meet with the Pope, but "Dylan was interested in meeting Leo, and Leo was completely open to it." Dylan and his entourage were scheduled to arrive at 3:45 p.m. but were 15 minutes early. They had to wait until 4:20 p.m., then went up to the Pope's apartment in the palace known as the Terza Loggia. "I felt the thrill of living through a meeting that had the taste of history, with the sense that anything could happen at every step," Spadaro told Padgett. "The Pope and Dylan sat down at a table in the library, like two old friends." He wouldn't or couldn't say what Dylan and Leo discussed, "But the way they looked at each other was beautiful, intense."

Spadaro added that there was no problem with Dylan's attire: "My impression was that, for Leo, the way Bob was dressed was entirely natural. No surprise at all. Besides, it was a private audience, not a formal one. No advance notice had been given." He also provided this nice summary of the Pope's history with Dylan:

In April, in Cameroon, he echoed the themes of “Masters of War.” In July he used the lines of “Go Away You Bomb” to speak out against nuclear rearmament. Leo XIV is an Augustinian, and in 1967, on John Wesley Harding, Dylan dreamed he saw that very saint. The Pope was born in Chicago in 1955 and was a teenager at the turn of the sixties and seventies. The American pop, folk, and rock of that era has been part of his cultural makeup since he was young. But it was Jim Musselman, Prevost’s classmate at Villanova University and a Bob Dylan admirer, who revealed that the two of them talked about music a lot. He was the one who told him to read an essay arguing that Dylan was the great poetic talent of his generation.

Dylan has some history with Christianity himself, though mostly not of the Catholic variety. After becoming a born-again Christian in 1978, he released a trio of religious album, 1979's Slow Train Coming, 1980's Saved, and 1981's Shot Of Love. On "Bob Dylan's 115th Dream" from 1965's Bringing It All Back Home, his narrative included the lines, "I said, 'For the Pope of Eruke I was employed'/ They let me go right away/ They were very paranoid."

Check out some more Dylan-meets-the-Pope pictures below.

And here's Dylan with Spadaro, who personally received a ticket to tonight's show in Rome from the man himself:

entry.summary: Things aren’t looking good for KATSEYE. On Tuesday (Nov. 3), the girl group canceled their sold-out Detroit concert just 30 minutes before showtime, citing Megan’s illness. Now, they’ve canceled tonight’s Chicago show last-minute, too. The venue announced the cancellation on social media, writing, “We’re sorry to share that tonight’s KATSEYE show at the United Center…
entry.content:
Things aren't looking good for KATSEYE. On Tuesday (Nov. 3), the girl group canceled their sold-out Detroit concert just 30 minutes before showtime, citing Megan's illness. Now, they've canceled tonight's Chicago show last-minute, too.

The venue announced the cancellation on social media, writing, "We're sorry to share that tonight's KATSEYE show at the United Center has been postponed due to Megan's illness. Please do not travel to the venue, as doors will not open for tonight's show. We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience."

"Please hold on to your tickets," the statement continued. "They'll be valid for the new date, which we'll announce soon. VIP packages, including soundcheck upgrades, will carry over too. If you can't make the new date, refunds will be available to your original payment method. Thank you for your patience and understanding."

In August, KATSEYE dropped off Olivia Rodrigo's inaugural Daisy Chain Festival due to Megan spraining her ankle during tour rehearsal. Meanwhile, two out of the six members — Manon and Sophia — are on hiatus.

entry.content:
Martin Meyer, the St. Louis musician who used to head up the lo-fi punk label Lumpy Records and the equally lo-fi punk band Lumpy And The Dumpers, has moved on from lumping and dumping and is now apparently very passionate about soup. His new project is called Soup Activists, and his latest batch of tuneful power-pop under that name, Where The Rubbish Goes, arrives next week. While lead single "Johnny" was a fired-up blast of jangling guitar, "The Castle" is mellower and dreamier. Check it out below.

Where The Rubbish Goes is out 11/13 on Feel It Records.

entry.summary: Jess Kerber’s The World Is Dark, But I Want It To Be Funny arrives tomorrow. So far the Nashville-based singer-songwriter has shared the evocative singles “Changing” and “Louisiana Song.” Now, she’s back with the title track featuring Emily Hines. “This song came from a place of realizing that every single time I have tried to…
entry.content:
Jess Kerber's The World Is Dark, But I Want It To Be Funny arrives tomorrow. So far the Nashville-based singer-songwriter has shared the evocative singles "Changing" and "Louisiana Song." Now, she's back with the title track featuring Emily Hines.

"This song came from a place of realizing that every single time I have tried to find humor or focus on the casualness of daily activities in whatever bad situation I am in, it's helped me to accept the bigger picture," Kerber explains. "That's not to say that low moments have to be intellectualized or not validated, but living in a time where so many levels of humanity are constantly being challenged, we have to look inward and be more creative in the ways that we pick ourselves back up.  As much as darkness is an inevitability, so is all of the lightness."

Watch the live studio video of "The World Is Dark, But I Want It To Be Funny" below.

The World Is Dark, But I Want It To Be Funny is out 11/6 on Felte.

entry.title: 1tbsp Announce New Album big soaps: Hear “Carottes”
entry.summary: Maxwell Byrne, the producer formerly known as Golden Vessel, has announced a new dance album as 1tbsp. Hear "Carottes" featuring Miki.
entry.content:
Maxwell Byrne, the Australian musician and producer who used to make electro-pop as Golden Vessel, has now announced his third full-length album of dance music under the name 1tbsp. Along with "Wish You Luck," his recent effervescent single featuring kid on air, the forthcoming big soaps will include multiple collaborations with Colombian-American artist Soltera, Venezuelan-Australian artist Cherry Chola, and French-Korean artist Miki. Today, he's sharing one of the latter, "Carottes." As Byrne explains:

miki and i only had two hours, we had a small overlap when i arrived in paris before she left for a tour, but in that short time we wrote three songs (two of which are on big soaps). we really clicked instantly, miki has great taste. she makes all these little snippets of found audio that she collects and edits on ableton. she very generously gave me some, and carottes started with me cutting up her soundbyte to make the main synth chords. at the time i was listening to a lot of greek music and i had came across this 2007 album, remastered 1 by stereo nova, that was a big inspiration for this song.

Listen and watch the accompanying music video below, and check out big soaps' tracklist and 1tbsp's upcoming tour dates while you're at it.

entry.content:
Last year, the Ophelias released their great third album Spring Grove. Today, bandleader Spencer Peppet is sharing "Power," her first new solo music in nine years.

The track is produced by Calvin Lauber and has sampling by Jevin Almazan. About it, Peppet says, "Why are all drinks $18 now? What is that? A drink should be $10. This song is about watching beautiful people at a fancy event and feeling like I don't belong, and then getting mad about something else entirely."

"Power" is shrouded in shoegazy fuzz and full of relatable, clever lines: "I'm funny when I'm by myself/ And grating when I open my mouth," Peppet laments. It comes with a music video made by Peppet with her Ophelias bandmate Jo Schaffer. Watch below.

entry.title: Troubling Details About NewJeans’ Exploitative Contracts Come To Light
entry.summary: South Korean pop music is a global commercial force with a factory-style star system, and the K-pop industry’s big record labels have come under increasing scrutiny for their insanely exploitative business practices. K-pop labels find talented kids, put them through intense rehearsals, arrange them into groups, and work them hard without giving them much money…
entry.content:
South Korean pop music is a global commercial force with a factory-style star system, and the K-pop industry's big record labels have come under increasing scrutiny for their insanely exploitative business practices. K-pop labels find talented kids, put them through intense rehearsals, arrange them into groups, and work them hard without giving them much money or artistic freedom. Some have died by suicide. The story of the K-pop girl group NewJeans is some of the most downright evil shit I have encountered in all my years covering this stuff. Now that a New York Times piece has revealed some of the terms of the group's contract, that story has become even more nightmarish.

When NewJeans debuted in 2022, they were the most exciting thing to happen to K-pop in a long time. The group arrived with a fully formed aesthetic, a take on the fizzily twee but futuristic dance-pop sound of artists like PinkPantheress. Singles like "Super Shy" and "OMG" were major international hits. Great songs, too. NewJeans were signed and assembled by Min Hee-jin, CEO of Ador, a subsidiary of Hybe, the gigantic label behind acts like BTS and KATSEYE. Min was pushed out of Ador after an internal label struggle, and NewJeans tried to leave the label with her. Last year, NewJeans announced that they were leaving Ador and changing their name to NJZ — an extremely rare case of a K-pop act pushing back against its label. It blew up in their faces.

NewJeans claimed that Ador voided their contract by mistreating and harassing them. The label sued, and a Korean court sided with Ador, ruling that the group could not quit. NewJeans promptly announced a hiatus, and the label fired one member, 20-year-old Danielle Marsh, and sued her for $22 million in what's known as "exit fees" — the penalties that Korean labels are contractually allowed to charge their artists if either side ends the contract. According to the Times, Marsh's exit fees were based on average monthly earnings, with the calculations only taking into account the months in which the group was making money.

The members of NewJeans were all children when Ador put them under contract; their parents had to sign for them. They lived in company dorms and trained around the clock, and four of the six members dropped out of school. A South Korean government contract template guarantees rights to physical and mental health, education, and sleep, but the Times reports that NewJeans contracts' eliminated those stipulations. When one NewJeans member's mother asked for changes in the contract, Ador's vice president reportedly replied, "If you do not agree to the current contract draft, including the points above, it may be best to reconsider the contract itself." The mother gave in and signed.

Apparently, K-pop labels frequently suggest plastic surgery procedures for young artists. (Plastic surgery is extremely popular in South Korea.) Per the Times, "The NewJeans contract required members to repay a significant share of what the label spent on plastic surgery and other beauty treatments while they were trainees." Hybe's representatives tell the Times, "We do not even recommend cosmetic surgery or procedures against an individual’s wishes."

NewJeans' contracts prohibited the singers from stating "true or false facts" that could damage the label's reputation, as well as things like underage drinking, drug use, "insincere attitude,” “neglect of self-management,” and “inappropriate romantic relationships." These are all apparently standard in K-pop. Other stipulations are much less common. NewJeans' contract runs out in 2029, but the label has allowed itself to keep using and licensing their identities for things like voice clones and AI chatbots. The label is also allowed to continue to sell and repackage their music after the contract ends while paying them a smaller share of royalties, another unusual twist.

The entire situation is bleak and nightmarish, and you can read the full exposé here. Free NewJeans.

Surely you've heard of Lex Walton, whose Sub Pop debut ULTIMATE LOVE FOREVER has been taking the indie world by storm. But Walton isn't just a musician — she's also an actress and a Facebook Marketplace addict. With a collection of secondhand gear, she's already recorded 35-40 demos for her next record. We sent Stereogum Deals Correspondent Rachel Brown to accompany Walton to snag a broken fuzz-wah pedal for the DIY power-pop artist's "trash finder's pile."

ULTIMATE LOVE FOREVER will get a physical release later this month. In Brown's chat with Walton, the two musicians talk record labels, being online, getting into playing music, and, of course, gear. Watch below.

entry.title: Toro y Moi Announces New Album Unusua: Hear “Motive”
entry.summary: Toro Y Moi first came to prominence as a chillwave pioneer, and he has explored a whole lot of different musical ideas over the past decade and a half. In the time since his 2024 album Hole Erth, Chaz Bear has done a lot of different things — covering Broken Social Scene, collaborating with Kenny…
entry.content:
Toro Y Moi first came to prominence as a chillwave pioneer, and he has explored a whole lot of different musical ideas over the past decade and a half. In the time since his 2024 album Hole Erth, Chaz Bear has done a lot of different things — covering Broken Social Scene, collaborating with Kenny Beats, demonstrating an AI music tool at an AI developer conference. We can only hope that he didn't use that tool while making Unusua, the new album that he'll release in a couple of weeks.

A couple of weeks ago, Toro Y Moi released "Proof," a zoned-out instrumental that combines a still, impressionistic piano with a brittle, itchy synth arpeggio. Today, Bear quietly announced plans to release Unusua, simply by putting the album listing up on Bandcamp without elaborating. We haven't received any PR on the record. According to the Bandcamp page, Bear performed, arranged, and produced the entire record himself at Scenic Route in Berkeley and 2200 Studios in Sausalito.

Based on "Proof" and "Motive," the new track that Bundick shared today, it looks like Unusua will be a piano-heavy instrumental record. Below, check out those two tracks and the LP's tracklist.

entry.title: Of Course Grimes Is In The First AI Film To Screen In US Theaters
entry.summary: Despite overwhelming evidence to the contrary, various moneyed interests continue to believe that people actually want to watch AI-generated movies. In the past few years, some filmmakers have humiliated themselves by experimenting with AI, ending up with things like Steven Soderbergh’s John Lennon documentary that got viciously panned at Cannes earlier this year. Now, a…
entry.content:
Despite overwhelming evidence to the contrary, various moneyed interests continue to believe that people actually want to watch AI-generated movies. In the past few years, some filmmakers have humiliated themselves by experimenting with AI, ending up with things like Steven Soderbergh's John Lennon documentary that got viciously panned at Cannes earlier this year. Now, a fully AI-generated movie is set to open in US theaters, and you will not be shocked to learn that Grimes is involved.

Zack London, a YouTuber who goes by the name Gossip Goblin, is the force behind Gods Don't Give Gifts, a new AI-generated sci-fi anthology. London is independently distributing the movie, which is set to open Dec. 4, and he's also submitting it for Best Animated Film Oscar contention. AI-generated movies have screened in other countries, but this is apparently the first one to get a US theatrical release. We're blazing trails over here.

According to Variety, Gods Don't Give Gifts takes place in the "science-fiction, horror-tinged world of the 'Second Cycle of Humanity' where transhumanism has accelerated to the point that humanity looks very different." Here's the utterly incomprehensible trailer, which made me want call in sick for the rest of the day and go just lie down for a while.

Y! Entertainment describes Grimes' appearance in Gods Don't Give Gifts as a "cameo." If you make a cameo in an AI-generated movie, do you actually have to show up someplace and perform in front of a camera? Or do you just have to sign off on it, and then someone types your name into a prompt? Here's how a press release describes her character: "Grimes plays Zayinth Alda — a disaffected NiiroCore aristocrat and niece to Caen Halvorith, inventor of the Substrate Migration Protocol — who pays a visit to a dealer of dreamspools in the slums of East Cinder." I have been staring at that sentence for a few minutes now. The letters dance in front of my eyes. My brain is pure static. Nothing means anything.

Hey, we've got a clip! Check it out! Grimes as Zayinth Alda, a disaffected NiiroCore aristocrat and niece to Caen Halvorith, inventor of the Substrate Migration Protocol! Let's go!

Cinema! Is Grimes' acting AI-enhanced in some way, or is she just that good?

entry.content:
Liquid Mike, baby! What a band! How do they do it? How is it possible to continue cranking out banger after banger, never letting the energy or the quality dip? Back when they were toiling in remote obscurity, Mike Maple's Marquette, Michigan rock 'n' roll band quickly cranked out a whole series of shockingly sharp records. Now that they're out on the touring circuit, new Liquid Mike tracks don't come quite as quickly. But whenever there's a new one, you can be assured that it'll go hard.

Liquid Mike released their most recent album Hell Is An Airport a little more than a year ago, and their one-off single "Drowning Machine" came out in May. Right now, they're out on tour with Oso Oso, and they've got another new single. "Inanimate Object" is a giddy, hooky, fuzzed-out power-pop rave-up about what happens to you when you die. It rocks so hard. Check out the song's Bob Sweeney-directed video below.

entry.content:
Long before Geese became the biggest band in indie rock, the band's guitarist Emily Green teamed with Sunflower Bean's Olive Faber to form Star's Revenge. The band, which released its self-titled debut album in 2022, plays a scrappy, catchy, immensely appealing combination of garage rock and indie-pop. Today they're back with news of a second LP, and it's coming soon.

Star's Revenge II will be out three weeks from now, on Black Friday. Our first preview is "Don't Worry Dynamite," a Faber-sung tune with serious momentum, abundant charm, and some slide guitar that pushes the whole operation over the top. It's essentially twee classic rock, like the Replacements if they'd somehow ended up on Sarah Records.

"Don't Worry Dynamite" arrives with a video by Faber and Arielle Herman. Watch it below.

entry.title: Rush Announce Sphere Residency
entry.summary: In what seems like the most obvious combination of artist and venue that anyone could ever imagine, Rush have signed on to play some shows at Sphere in Las Vegas. The legendary prog band’s upcoming five-show Sphere residency is called Elevate From The Norm, and it goes down next May. I bet it’ll look trippy.…
entry.content:
In what seems like the most obvious combination of artist and venue that anyone could ever imagine, Rush have signed on to play some shows at Sphere in Las Vegas. The legendary prog band's upcoming five-show Sphere residency is called Elevate From The Norm, and it goes down next May. I bet it'll look trippy.

Right now, Geddy Lee and Alex Lifeson, the two surviving Rush members, are out on their Fifty Something tour. It's their first time on the road since their bandmate Neil Peart's 2020 death, and the rapturously received shows have included fun surprises like the show where they played their seven-part suite "2112" live for the first time in 29 years. Press materials promise "a set of fan favorites and greatest hits from across their catalogue." Here's what Lee says about the residency:

When I first heard of Sphere, I thought to myself, "Wow, what a shame that Rush is no longer touring, because this venue sounds tailor made for the kind of visual attitude with which we have always designed our shows." Normally, we spend months designing the visual effects for our shows, and this scenario seemed like the cherry on top of the ice cream for our design team. But life is nothing if not surprising, and now here we are, living and touring in the present tense, and we are able to make that particular dream come true. We are presently working hard to expand our touring concepts and concoct some new madness to suit this incredible venue and musically perform the kind of show we’ve been doing in some of our "one off" cities. Meaning playing all of 2112 and all of Moving Pictures, along with an array of other songs. We are so effin’ excited to make use of this incredible opportunity to please our fans both visually and viscerally — from wherever they might fly in from. Gonna be so much fun!!

Rush's Sphere shows are happening May 21, 23, 26, 28, and 30. Tickets go on sale 11/13 at 10 a.m. Pacific right here.

entry.content:
They already made a 2Pac biopic. It was called All Eyez On Me, and it came out in 2017. (I haven't seen the movie, but its reputation is not good.) In that picture, Danai Gurira played the role of Pac's mother Afeni Shakur, a storied figure in her own right. Now, another gifted actor will play the role of Afeni Shakur in a completely different biopic for a West Coast rap great. Cyntia Erivo is set to star as Afeni in Snoop, director Craig Brewer's upcoming film about Snoop Dogg's life.

Last year, the Outer Banks star signed on to play the titular role in Snoop, the upcoming biopic from Hustle & Flow/Song Sung Blue director Craig Brewer. The cast grew to include people like Lauren London as Snoop's mother Beverly Tate, Myles Bullock as Dr. Dre, Camron Jones as 2Pac, and Algee Smith as Warren G. In September, we learned that D'Angelo and Angie Stone's son SwayvoTwain had been cast as the Notorious B.I.G. Now, Variety reports that Cynthia Erivo, now the most famous person in the Snoop cast by quite some distance, will play Afeni Shakur.

Cynthia Erivo is a three-time Oscar nominee who has portrayed towering figures like Harriet Tubman and Aretha Franklin. She'll also play Miriam Makeba in The Road Home, an upcoming movie about the South African musicians on Paul Simon's Graceland tour. She also looks a lot like Afeni Shakur. But it's worth asking: Was Afeni Shakur really that important in Snoop Dogg's life? Will Erivo actually play a significant role in Snoop, or is this just a stunt-casting cameo?

Afeni Shakur, who died in 2016, might've had a more dramatically compelling life story than Snoop Dogg. She was a former Black Panther who successfully defended herself in the rest of the Panther 21 group in a famous New York conspiracy trial while she was pregnant with Tupac. So who knows, maybe this will be Erivo teasing a spinoff, Marvel-style. Snoop is scheduled to open next August, so I guess we'll find out then.

entry.content:
In November 1973, mere weeks after the release of his double-LP blockbuster Goodbye Yellow Brick Road, Elton John released an original holiday single called "Step Into Christmas." The song was a top-10 hit in the UK, and since 1995 it's been slotted onto the end of his 1974 album Caribou as a bonus track.

Today, more than 50 years after the original, he's released a new duet version of "Step Into Christmas" that pairs him with CMAT, the talented and charismatic Irish pop/country/alternative artist who we like quite a bit here at the Gum. She teased the collab by dressing as Elton John for Halloween, a move I appreciate as someone who posts a roundup of new Christmas albums for Halloween each year.

The new "Step Into Christmas" premieres today as part of the Amazon Music Holiday Originals campaign. In addition to the Elton John x CMAT duet, the series includes the Beaches covering Darlene Love's "Christmas (Baby Please Come Home)," the Head And The Heart doing Stevie Wonder's "Someday At Christmas," and a bunch of other tracks from artists like Hoshi, Elvis Crespo, Jalen Ngonda, MEEK, and Raya Real.

Check out the reworked "Step Into Christmas" at Amazon Music.

entry.title: Morphine – “Spaceman Charm”
entry.summary: In 1999, the unbelievably cool, permanently underrated Boston band Morphine ended in the most sudden, dramatic, tragic way that a band can end: Frontman Mark Sandman had a heart attack and died while playing a show in Italy. Morphine released one more album, 2000’s The Night, which was completed before Sandman’s passing. Now, we’re about…
entry.content:
In 1999, the unbelievably cool, permanently underrated Boston band Morphine ended in the most sudden, dramatic, tragic way that a band can end: Frontman Mark Sandman had a heart attack and died while playing a show in Italy. Morphine released one more album, 2000's The Night, which was completed before Sandman's passing. Now, we're about to get another Morphine album, made from the recordings that Sandman left behind.

Morphine's upcoming album Cocoon is built from a series of abandoned recordings that Mark Sandman made with longtime Morphine producers Paul Q. Kolderie and Sean Slade in the last years of his life. Kolderie and Sandman's partner Sabine Hrechdakian have gone through those recordings and constructed an album from them, and band member Dana Colley returned to record new saxophone parts for some of those songs. Versions of many of the songs, including the lead-single title track, already came out on the 2004 double CD Sandbox: The Music Of Mark Sandman. Today, we get to hear a Morphine track that's never been released in any form.

Morphine recorded "Spaceman Charm" in 1998, and it's exactly the sort of seductive, atmospheric jazz-rock that made the band such a powerful force. This is one of the songs with a new saxophone part from Dana Colley, but I couldn't tell that from listening to it. It could've absolutely fit on a classic like Cure For Pain. Here's what Colley says about it:

I struggled at first with what to add to "Spaceman Charm." These recordings had been set aside when we moved on to what became The Night, and coming back to them all these years later felt like resuscitating something from the past. With Paul Kolderie's guidance, I began experimenting with different saxophones and bass clarinet, finding ways to build on what Mark had recorded. Ultimately, it was a sense of completion, finally finishing something we'd started together nearly three decades ago.

Check it out below.

Cocoon is out 12/4 on Partisan.

entry.content:
Pearl Jam's whole drummer situation is still up in the air. The band has had a number of drummers over the years, and the longest-tenured of them just left the band last year. Matt Cameron, also of Soundgarden, announced that he was departing Pearl Jam after 27 years in July 2025. (Cameron has since rejoined Soundgarden and played sets at their Rock And Roll Hall Of Fame induction and the NFL's season opener, and there are rumors of a 2027 tour.) Pearl Jam, meanwhile, found a temporary replacement for Cameron, but they haven't yet named a permanent member of the band.

In September, Pearl Jam played two sets at Eddie Vedder's Ohana Festival, their first since Cameron left the band. For those shows, Pearl Jam brought in Abe Laboriel Jr., a 55-year-old session musician and a member of Paul McCartney's touring band. During the show, Vedder introduced Laboriel and thanked him for "helping us out on drums tonight." In a statement after the festival, the band thanked Laboriel for "sitting in on drums," which also seems to suggest that his time with the band was temporary. Now, bassist Jeff Ament has shed a little more light on the situation.

Ament recently published a new photo book called Since Forever, and that's why he did a recent Under The Radar interview. Naturally, the subject of Pearl Jam's drummer position came up. Apparently, Pearl Jam are still auditioning drummers. Ament describes "Laboriel as "such an incredible drummer," but the band is still trying to figure out future plans. He says:

We're not in any massive rush, but we want to play some shows next year. I'm 63, but I'm pretty fit. I think I can act like a young foolish guy up there for a few more years, but I feel a little bit more urgency in terms of getting out there to play shows when we are physically young-ish.

Ament also addressed Matt Cameron's departure:

I think when Chris [Cornell] passed, that was a massive hit for all of us, but in particular for Matt. I know there was a period of time where he wasn't sure he wanted to even play anymore, and pretty much since then he's been talking about winding it down and wanting to do some other things. He's got some other itches to scratch but it was a pretty fucking sad moment... You've got years of traveling the world and making music together, but I'm stoked for him.

Read the interview here.
